B: Hiya! Can you hear me okay? I've had these headphones since about 2015, so they might be on their way out.
A: Yes, I can hear you. I'm Abena.
B: Neil, nice to meet you. I'm in Shipley, near Bradford. How did you get on with that puzzle at the start? I got completely stuck on the third one.
A: The one with the shapes? I just guessed that one, honestly. I didn't have the patience.
B: Ha, glad it's not just me. Where are you calling from?
A: Crawley. You know, near Gatwick.
B: Oh right, so you'll get the planes going over.
A: All day. But you stop hearing them, that's the funny thing. People come to my house and they're like, how do you live with this? And I say, live with what?
B: That's like me with the trains. The Airedale line runs at the bottom of our road, and I couldn't tell you when one goes past. I could tell you how late they are, mind. So what do you do down there?
A: I'm a pharmacy technician. Community pharmacy in the town centre, three days a week. Dispensing, checking scripts, ringing the GP surgeries when they've sent something wrong. That's a lot of my day, to be honest.
B: Oh, that's not a million miles off me. I'm a lab technician at a university, chemistry teaching labs. Basically I'm the bloke who makes sure the fume cupboards work and the students don't poison themselves.
A: Okay, so you know what it's like, everything has to be logged.
B: Oh, everything. COSHH forms, stock, the lot. I'm quite sad about it really, I sort of enjoy a tidy log.
A: See, I'm the opposite. The actual dispensing I'm fast, I'll spot a wrong dose straight away. But the paperwork, erm, it piles up. I've been told off about the controlled drugs register more than once.
B: Well, that's the important bit done well, isn't it? The dose. Nobody ever died of a late register.
A: Tell that to my area manager.
B: Ha! Fair. Are you from Crawley originally?
A: No, Ghana. Kumasi. I came to London at nineteen, then moved to Crawley because the rent was cheaper. That was a long time ago now.
B: Kumasi, that's the Asante region, isn't it? I've read a bit about the Asante kingdom. Sorry, I'm a history nerd, I read anything I can get hold of.
A: Yes, that's right. You know more than most people, I'll give you that.
B: Not much more, honestly. One book and a documentary. So what do you do when you're not at work?
A: I've got two kids, so mostly that. Football on Saturday with my son. Church on Sunday, which always goes on too long.
B: Oh, I'm a chapel-goer myself. Methodist. Ours is pretty brisk, it has to be, half the congregation's over eighty.
A: Mine's Methodist too, a Ghanaian congregation. But brisk, no. If it finishes in two and a half hours, that's a good week.
B: Two and a half hours! We'd lose people. Literally, some of them wouldn't make it.
A: You'd love it, though, the singing is very good.
B: Now you're talking. I sing bass in a choir in Saltaire, so you've got my attention there. Is it hymns, or more
A: Both, and some highlife-style ones, my mum's
